learning_objectives: Explain the *structure of this course* and identify the core concepts (evolution definition, importance of scale, process vs pattern).
Identify *key components and organelles* in cells critical to understanding evolution (DNA, nucleus, ER, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, chloroplasts), and state their purposes.
Define the *central dogma of biology*. Explain how cells can turn genetic material into traits, and the molecules involved in that process (see first-day notes).
Define the basic terms used to discuss *genetics* (see first-day notes).
Define the basic terms used to discuss *taxonomy and phylogenetics* (see first-day notes).
Identify the *12 focal species* that will be used in this class from their latin names (see first-day notes).

reading: Read 1.1 (but skip any subsection whose title starts with "How Does...")
Read 1.2 (but skip last two subsections "Understanding Evolution..." and "The Evolution of HIV...")
learning_objectives: \* Interpret *data from graphs* by identifying axis quantities and identifying patterns from visualizations.
\* Identify key parts of the *life cycle for HIV* in human cells, with focus on the entry receptor & co-receptor and what happens to the virus's genetic material in the cell.
\* Describe the *role of reverse transcriptase* for HIV.
\* Explain how *AZT blocks reverse transcriptase*.
\* Identify two ways that reverse transcriptase might *evolve resistance to AZT*, and which was observed to occur.
\* Describe how errors during replication of the reverse transcriptase gene can lead to *changes in the frequency of drug resistance* in a host's HIV particles.

questions.body: Which of the following correctly describes why HIV can be treated by AZT? FYI: for this question, the first part of each option is a true statement, but the second part is only true for one option. Questions like this are common in this class, so make sure you read options all the way through.
options: HIV's reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA; AZT looks like a DNA nucleotide but can't be added to once integrated.
HIV's capsid proteins bind to the CD4 receptor protein; AZT permanently binds to CD4, removing the viral entry point.
HIV's integrase protein integrates viral DNA into host DNA; AZT binds to integrase's allosteric site, inactivating it.
HIV's proteases break apart proteins into subcomponents to activate them; AZT looks like a protein cleavage site but permanently binds to the proteases's active site.

questions.body: Which of the following best describes how HIV might become resistant to drugs like AZT?
options: While copying viral genetic material, HIV proteins can make mistakes. A small percentage of these mistakes happen to confer partial or full resistance to antiviral drugs, so they have more success replicating and become more common.

When faced with antiviral drugs, HIV can detect its own weaknesses. If it is able to survive the encounter with the drug, it makes adjustments to its genetic material so future progeny will be more successful.
In the presence of antiviral drugs, HIV can choose to become dormant. Doing so allows the drug to naturally decompose until it is at a low enough concentration that it is no longer effective.

Antiviral drugs can only do so much damage to HIV. After a certain threshold of damage is inflicted on HIV particles, they are no longer affected by the drug. They stabilize and continue replicating at this point, albeit at a reduced rate.

questions.body: Which of the following is correct about what happens to viral genetic material during the life cycle of HIV?
options: HIV virions carry RNA and proteins; one of its proteins convert its RNA to DNA; another one of its proteins integrates the DNA into the host cell's genome; the host cell makes viral RNA from the integrated viral DNA; that RNA is integrated into new virions
HIV virions carry RNA and proteins; one of its proteins makes copies of the RNA; that RNA is integrated into new virions
HIV virions carry DNA and proteins; the host cell's proteins makes viral RNA from that DNA; the host cell also makes copies of the viral DNA; that DNA is integrated into new virions
HIV virions carry DNA and proteins; one of its proteins integrates the DNA into the host cell's genome; the host cell makes copies of the integrated viral DNA; that DNA is integrated into new virions

reading: Read 1.3 (but skip last three subsections "A Missing...", "Practical...", and "An Unresolved...")
Read 1.4 (but skip last two subsections "The Origin..." and "When Did...")
Read Computing Consequences 1.1 (titled "When did HIV...", p24)
learning_objectives: \* State the reason that the alleles *CCR5-∆32 and C868T* (from different genes) are named as such and how they are significant to HIV immunity.
\* Compare the *rates of evolution* between viruses and their hosts.
Demonstrate how point mutations in viruses over time can be *represented by an evolutionary tree*.
\* Interpret the *relatedness of viral variants* from an evolutionary tree. Identify closely- and distantly-related pairs of variants.
\* Explain how evolutionary trees can determine the likely *source of infection* in one host from a set of potential infecting hosts.
\* Describe how *modernly observed mutation rates* can give evidence for how long ago HIV jumped from chimpanzees to humans.

questions.body: With respect to the phylogenetic tree to the right, which of the following is true about the taxa B? (see image at https://miles-1.github.io/26c-fa_evolution/tree_quiz.svg) NOTE: I don't like this question any more because the structure implies that genetic divergence is being represented by branch length. Everyone got full credit for this one.
options: B is most closely related to C; B is equally distantly related to A and D
B is most closely related to C; B is most distantly related to D
B is most closely related to A; B is equally distantly related to C and D
B is most closely related to A; B is most distantly related to D

questions.body: CCR5-∆32 is an allele for the CCR5 gene. Where does it get its name?
options: Compared to the wild type allele, CCR5-∆32 has 32 base pairs deleted from it
Compared to the wild type allele, CCR5-∆32 has 32 point mutations
The initial study that identified CCR5-∆32 only found it in 32 patients
CCR5-∆32 is known to change the expression of 32 other genes related to HIV immunity

questions.body: How can mutation rates observed in HIV today be used to approximate when HIV and SIV (the chimpanzee's equivalent to HIV) first diverged?
options: We know the approximate genetic divergence between HIV and the common ancestor of HIV and SIV; the rate at which divergence increases over time gives evidence for when divergence was zero.
High mutation rates indicate that the common ancestor of HIV and SIV must have occurred recently, as fast mutation over long periods of time is bound to destroy HIV.

High mutation rates indicate that the common ancestor of HIV and SIV must have existed around the time of the common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans, as it must adapt quickly to changes in both species.

SIV is genetically identical to the common ancestor of HIV and SIV; HIV's fast mutation rate indicates it was recently genetically identical to SIV and evolutionary forces are pushing to differentiate them.

reading: Read 2.1 (but skip subsection "Evidence from Direct Observation...")
learning_objectives: \* Explain the mechanism of how *selective breeding* can bring about changes in the genetics of a population.
\* Define *vestigial structures*: explain why they are evidence of descent with modification and why they remain despite having virtually no use.
\* Name and describe *five examples of vestigial structures* (specifically: kiwi wings, python spurs, human coccyx/arrector pili & stickleback pelvic structures)
\* State the *common name* of _Gasterosteus aculeatus_ (one of our focal species, see first-day notes).

\* Demonstrate how *speciation is a gradual process* through four stickleback examples (Robert's Lake/Creek, Paxton Lake, Akkeshi Bay; names of water bodies not important, just qualitative differences of the four examples).
\* Define *"ring species"* and explain how examples of them challenge the idea of discrete species and demonstrate how one species might split into two.

questions.body: Which of the following accurately describes how selective breeding can bring about desired traits in a bred population?
options: A breeder selects individuals with desired traits to breed; mating individuals genetically amplify and exaggerate their traits in order to make it more likely to mate again, and those traits become more common
A breeder selects individuals with desired traits to breed; their traits are passed down to their offspring and become more common

A breeder physically morphs or augments selected individuals to have desired traits (e.g., cutting away ugly leaves from plants); those traits are embedded genetically in those individuals and passed on to future generations, and those traits become more common

A breeder physically morphs or augments selected individuals to have desired traits (e.g., cutting away ugly leaves from plants); this is repeated every generation regardless of population genetics, so those traits become more common

questions.body: What is the definition of a "ring species"?
options: A species that repeatedly cycles through a repeating set of genetic states over time because of delayed selective pressures experienced later in life. In early life, key survival traits are not expressed, thus delaying selection until later in life.
A species that repeatedly cycles through a repeating set of genetic states over time due to cyclically-repeating environmental conditions.

A species with a ring-shaped geographic range made of a connected series of neighboring populations. Each adjacent population can interbreed, except where the two ends of the ring meet, where those two populations are too distinct to mate.
A species with a ring-shaped geographic range where, despite large environmental differences across the range, all populations of the species can interbreed.

questions.body: What is the common name of _Gasterosteus aculeatus_?
options: Common house mouse
Blue-ringed octopus
Siberian greenish warbler
Three-spined stickleback

reading: Read 2.3 (but skip three sub-subsections: "A Fossil Transitional Bird", "Transitional Forms Allow...", and "A Transitional Turtle")
Read 2.4 (but skip two sub-subsections: "Molecular Homology" and "A Predictive Test...")
Read Computing Consequences 2.1 ("A closer look at radiometric dating")
learning_objectives: \* Define key *vocabulary* (specifically: fossil, transitional form, homology, uniformitarianism, radiometric dating)
\* Explain how the *Pacific leaping blenny* (amazing name) demonstrates that organisms can evolve to survive in very different environments than their ancestors.
\* Identify three cases where species have similar traits (vertebrate forelimbs, fins/flippers in sharks/orcas, orchid flower parts) and if they represent *homologous or non-homologous* traits.
\* Hypothesize the *relatedness between a set of species using homologous traits*.
\* Order key species by *most-to-least related to humans* (specifically: frog, chimp, alligator, cat, sea urchin, stickleback, fruit fly).
\* Calculate the *age of a biological sample* from the parent-daughter ratio of isotopes (given the initial parent-daughter ratio and the half-life time of the parent isotope).

questions.body: Which of the following is the correct definition of the term "homology" in an evolutionary context?
options: The study of homosexuality (or more generally, non-heterosexuality) in animals.
The study of repeated patterns across the genotypes of unrelated species.
The study of similar structures in species, which indicates their relatedness.
The study of transitional amphibious organisms that are thought to descend from water-dwelling organisms.

questions.body: Which of the following correctly describes the Pacific leaping blenny's evolutionary history?
options: Blennies are *amphibious*, and are thought to have descended from *pelagic* (open water) organisms, which themselves descend from *benthic* (deep water) organisms
Blennies are *aquatic*, and are thought to have descended from *hyporheic* (just below stream bed) organisms, who themselves descend from *fossorial* (underground) organisms
Blennies are *aerial*, and are thought to have descended from *arboreal* (tree-dwelling) organisms, which themselves descend from *terrestrial* organisms
Blennies are *terrestrial*, and are thought to have descended from *amphibious* organisms, which themselves descend from *aquatic* organisms

questions.body: Which of the following is correct about radiometric dating?
options: Individual radioactive atoms decay randomly, but masses of radioactive atoms altogether decay at a predictable rate overall, which can be used to measure the age of a sample.

Individual radioactive atoms decay sequentially (one at a time), starting at the surface of the mass and moving inwards as outer layers are shed; the size of the radioactive masses indicates the sample's age
In fossils, radioactive atoms naturally accumulate, and that rate of build-up indicates how long the sample has been fossilized
Masses of radioactive atoms generally persist indefinitely in organic samples, but become more radioactive over time, which can be used to measure the age of the sample

reading: Read the first part of Ch. 4
Read 4.1 (skim subsections "How to Read Time..." and "How to Read Relationships...", read rest thoroughly)
learning_objectives: Interpret the pattern of extant species diversity using *tree thinking* (i.e., in terms of the relationships between extant species and their genetic divergence).
\* Identify when two *evolutionary trees of different styles* or taxon orders demonstrate the same evolutionary information.
\* Explain why *evolutionary trees are considered hypotheses*.
\* Define key *vocabulary* (specifically: apomorphy, synapomorphy, plesiomorphy, monophyletic group/clade, paraphyletic, polyphyletic, polytomy).
\* Describe how including an *outgroup* in phylogenies can accurately root a tree (or, synonymously, can ensure the ingroup is monophyletic).
\* Define *parsimony* as a phylogenetic analysis method, and describe how true phylogenetic data might break the assumptions of parsimony (specifically: convergent evolution, reversals, homoplasy).

questions.body: Which of the following correctly describes these four trees? See https://miles-1.github.io/26c-fa_evolution/L06_quiz_trees.png for images.
options: Trees 2, 3, and 4 show the same information as each other, but show different information than tree 1.
Trees 1, 3, and 4 show the same information as each other, but show different information than tree 2.
Trees 1 & 2 show the same information as each other, as do 3 & 4, but 1 & 2 are different than 3 & 4.
Trees 1 & 3 show the same information as each other, as do 2 & 4, but 1 & 3 are different than 2 & 4.

questions.body: What is the difference between an apomorphy and a synapomorphy?
options: An *apomorphy* is a newly-evolved trait (relative to whatever you're studying); a *synapomorphy* is an apomorphy shared by two or more lineages that form their own clade
An *apomorphy* is an ancestral trait, whereas a *synapomorphy* is a more recently-evolved trait
A *synapomorphy* is an ancestral trait, whereas an *apomorphy* is a more recently-evolved trait
A *synapomorphy* is a newly-evolved trait (relative to whatever you're studying); an *apomorphy* is a synapomorphy shared by two or more lineages that form their own clade

questions.body: Which of the following is the definition of parsimony?
options: A method of tree analysis that prefers hypotheses where *more* evolutionary changes were made
A method of tree analysis that *maximizes* the number of clades in a tree
A method of tree analysis that *minimizes* the number of clades in a tree
A method of tree analysis that prefers hypotheses where *fewer* evolutionary changes were made
